transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I'm seeking help because I've been struggling with really distressing, intrusive memories and awful nightmares about a traumatic event that happened about a year and ten months ago. They just keep coming back, and I can't seem to get them out of my head.
Since the event, have you been avoiding reminders of it or feeling constantly on edge, jumpy, or easily startled?

Yes, I actively try to avoid any thoughts, memories, or places that remind me of the event. I'm also constantly on edge and get extremely startled by sudden noises or unexpected touches, and it takes a really long time for my heart to stop pounding afterward.
Have these symptoms been causing major problems in your daily life, like at work, in relationships, or with taking care of yourself?
Yes, they've been causing major problems. I've completely withdrawn from my friends and family, and I just don't have the motivation to do my work or complete daily tasks anymore.
Over the past two weeks, have you been feeling depressed most of the day or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, even when they are not related to the trauma?

Yes, I've completely lost interest in all the hobbies and activities I used to enjoy. Most of the time I just feel emotionally numb and flat, and I can't seem to experience any happiness or joy anymore, regardless of what is going on.
Do you also have strong trauma-related guilt, blame yourself or others for what happened, or feel detached from other people mainly since the trauma?

I feel incredibly detached and distant from everyone, and I've become so emotionally numb that I struggle to feel any love or affection for my family. However, I don't really experience strong feelings of guilt or blame myself for what happened.
Have you had thoughts that life is not worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?
No, I haven't had any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life. Even though everything feels really difficult and numb right now, I don't experience those kinds of thoughts.
Do you ever feel like the traumatic event is happening again in the moment, such as having flashbacks or becoming so upset by reminders that you lose track of your surroundings?

Yes, absolutely. I experience intense flashbacks where it genuinely feels like the trauma is happening all over again in real-time. Encountering anything that reminds me of it triggers such severe distress that I completely lose track of my current surroundings.
Before the traumatic event happened, had you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed most of the day or lost interest in nearly everything?
No, I don't recall ever having a period like that before the event happened. I really don't think I ever felt that way back then.
In the past two weeks, have you also had changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, or felt slowed down or unusually restless most days?
I haven't really noticed any changes in my appetite, energy, or concentration, and I don't feel physically restless or slowed down. I'm not really sure about those things, to be honest.
Aside from the trauma nightmares, have you had trouble sleeping most nights, like difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking very early?
I haven't really noticed any other specific sleep issues like having trouble falling asleep or waking up too early. It's really just the distressing nightmares that wake me up and disrupt my sleep.

The interview strongly supports Posttraumatic Stress Disorder because the patient describes a qualifying traumatic event nearly 2 years ago followed by intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance, hypervigilance/startle, detachment, emotional numbing, and significant functional impairment lasting well beyond 1 month. Major Depressive Disorder remains a candidate because there is marked anhedonia and emotional numbness, but it is less clearly established as a separate disorder since the patient denies a pre-trauma depressive episode and does not clearly endorse enough additional depressive symptoms such as appetite, energy, concentration, psychomotor, or broader sleep disturbance outside trauma nightmares. More questioning would be needed to determine whether depressive symptoms are better accounted for by PTSD versus a comorbid Major Depressive Disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a qualifying traumatic event followed by persistent intrusion symptoms (distressing memories, nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in mood/connection (detachment, emotional numbness, anhedonia), and hyperarousal (on edge, exaggerated startle) lasting about 1 year and 10 months with clear functional impairment. Major Depressive Disorder was considered because of anhedonia and emotional flatness, but the depressive symptoms appear trauma-linked and are not supported by a broader independent major depressive syndrome in the interview.
